justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a gently upward-sloping baseline across the three horizons, which is typical for an asset trading near recent support levels with no strong near-term catalysts in either direction. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the last observed price, assuming mean-reversion dominates over very short windows and that overnight or intraday noise would keep movement modest. For the one-week estimate, I applied a slight positive drift reflecting a modest bullish bias that often appears in equity or commodity markets during periods of low volatility regime. For the one-month estimate, the drift assumption compounds further, pushing the point estimate modestly higher, though the incremental gain per unit time shrinks as uncertainty begins to dominate the directional signal.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized volatility scaling. Over one day, historical daily ranges tend to be relatively tight in stable market conditions, so the 90% interval spans roughly 17 points. Over one week, I scaled by approximately the square root of five trading days, widening the band to about 36 points on each side. Over one month, the interval nearly doubles again, spanning roughly 76 points total, reflecting both the compounding of daily volatility and the increased probability of regime shifts or macro surprises materializing over a longer window. I also incorporated a modest fat-tail adjustment at the monthly horizon, recognizing that financial return distributions tend to have heavier tails than a pure Gaussian assumption would suggest.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic data surprises such as unexpected inflation prints or central bank policy shifts, which historically generate gap moves that can exceed several standard deviations in a single session. Geopolitical shocks, earnings announcements if this is an equity, or liquidity events such as month-end rebalancing flows could also create outsized moves. On the downside, a technical breakdown below key support levels could trigger stop-loss cascades and accelerate selling beyond the lower bound of any of my intervals.

It is also worth noting that my intervals carry inherent model risk. I assumed relatively stationary volatility, but volatility itself is mean-reverting and can spike sharply. If realized volatility over the forecast period turns out to be two or three times the baseline assumption, the actual distribution of outcomes would be far wider than stated, and my stated 90% confidence intervals would effectively undercover the true range of plausible outcomes.
